query: What metadata schema, centralized repository, SOP templates, and pre-registration format will govern synthesis and analysis, and who will own weekly synthesis updates and biweekly reviews?

response.query: What metadata schema, centralized repository, SOP templates, and pre-registration format will govern synthesis and analysis, and who will own weekly synthesis updates and biweekly reviews?
response.answer: The PRISMA and PROSPERO guidelines govern synthesis and analysis; protocols are registered on PROSPERO. SOP templates are available from various sources, and weekly updates are owned by the project lead. Biweekly reviews are conducted by the project team.

The review protocol is a critical document that outlines the methods and approach for conducting an evidence synthesis review, including eligibility criteria, data sources, and planned analysis. **Benefits of having a protocol for evidence synthesis:**. **The resources below include general guidelines and/or templates for writing an evidence synthesis protocol. * A practical guide to protocol development for systematic reviews. Ideally, you should **register your protocol before the literature searches have been executed**. **How do I register my protocol?**. Some registries, like PROSPERO, only accept systematic review protocols, while others may include additional functionality to track any research project from start to finish. **List of Registries That Accept Evidence Synthesis Protocols**. PROSPERO is a free resource that accepts protocols of systematic reviews that are relevant to human health. Scoping review protocols are not currently accepted in PROSPERO. Templates are available for different types of study registrations, including systematic reviews. * INPLASY - International Platform of Registered Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis protocols. INPLASY is a fee based platform that accepts "systematic review protocols assessing interventions, prognostic factors, diagnostic accuracy, methodological reviews, epidemiological reviews, and systematic reviews of animal studies. Additionally, INPLASY accepts systematic reviews assessing sports performance as an outcome, methodological reviews that evaluate the quality of reporting, pedagogical reviews, evidence and gap maps, mapping reviews, and scoping reviews.". Author instructions for submitting proposals for "new reviews, evidence and gap maps (EGMs), and methods research papers for publication in Campbell Systematic Reviews.". * JBI Protocol and Review Registration. Instructions for authors submitting protocols to JBI Evidence Synthesis journal. Includes links to repositories for pre-registration as well as protocol templates for different review types. Some journals will also accept and publish evidence synthesis protocols.

results.title: My Personal Weekly Reviews in Dendron - DEV Community
results.content: # My Personal Weekly Reviews in Dendron. Dendron is a VS Code extension and a "knowledge management tool". It's barely a context switch for me when I'm coding vs writing notes in Dendron. If you want to use Dendron as a team tool, you can check your dendron "vault" into a git repository and share it as any regular codebase. Dendron has a built-in daily journal feature that's easy to use. To do this, I create a "schema" and a "template". Schemas are a way to describe a file naming convention and which template to use when creating a new note with that convention. All dendron notes are in the same directory. The Dendron extension comes with its own sidebar and its own views. Dendron files use a dot-namespaced notation to build a virtual tree structure. For example, a file named `` will be a peer of `` and the two notes will be in the `foo` namespace. A common convention for managing templates is to put the notes in a 'templates' namespace. I press `ctrl+l` to create a note named '`templates.weekly-review`' with this text (loosely based on the David Allen's 'Getting Things Done' methodology):. Secondly, I create my weekly report schema file. I press `shift+ctrl+l` to create a new schema, and type in `weekly-review`. This create a new file called '``' and I type in my schema document:. You can see we defined a template named `` for the last schema part. Notes named in the format of: `weekly.report.2022.05.08` will match this schema. I press `ctrl-n` to create new note. I name it '`weekly.review.2022.05.08`' (you don't give it the `.md` extension) and it comes pre-populated with the template text we defined earlier. Now, every time I create weekly report note it is pre-populated with questions for me to answer. I can edit the template and it will be used for next week's report. I am still ramping up my usage of dendron, and my tree of notes is growing as I gather my thoughts outside my head and work toward managing my time and energy better:. Also, If you have ideas for a better weekly review template, I'd like to hear your suggestions.
